title: My Whole Life Is Thunder

jokes.text: Liz Lemon sings an improvised wedding song to announce her marriage: '# Married # # Liz Lemon got married # # And made up this song, doo-doo-doo doo-doo-doo doo-doo #'
jokes.setup: The episode opens with what sounds like it could be a formal announcement
jokes.punchline: It's Liz singing a completely improvised, nonsensical song about her own marriage — the song itself acknowledges it was made up on the spot
jokes.explanation: The self-referential nature ('made up this song') is a great meta-joke — Liz is so un-romantic that her wedding announcement is a dorky improvised ditty. Very character-specific: only Liz Lemon announces her marriage this way. Strong opening gag.

jokes.text: 'What the H-E-double-vibrator is that thing on your left hand?'
jokes.setup: Someone is about to say 'H-E-double-hockey-sticks' (a censored 'hell')
jokes.punchline: Instead of 'hockey sticks,' Frank substitutes 'vibrator' — a surprise escalation that's also anatomically punny
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever subversion of the children's censorship euphemism. The double meaning (the shape of a vibrator is like a double hockey stick) makes it earned rather than random, and the economy is superb — maximum shock from minimal syllables. One of the best single-line jokes in the episode. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jenna reveals she had a surprise wedding planned: 'You just ruined my surprise wedding!' — complete with Paul waiting upstairs and Reverend Gimp
jokes.setup: Liz is being chastised for getting married without telling anyone
jokes.punchline: Jenna was about to have her OWN surprise wedding, and the escalating details (Paul eating asparagus upstairs, 'Reverend Gimp') make it increasingly absurd
jokes.explanation: The concept is perfectly calibrated to Jenna's narcissism — of course she also planned a surprise wedding, and of course she'd eat asparagus in preparation. 'Reverend Gimp' is a perfect throwaway detail. The escalation of absurd details makes this a multi-layered joke rather than a single punchline.

jokes.text: 'I guess I ate all that asparagus for nothing.'
jokes.setup: Paul is coming down from wherever he was waiting for the surprise wedding
jokes.punchline: His primary concern is the wasted asparagus — implying it had a specific (sexual) purpose, played with complete deadpan resignation
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the implication is clear without being stated. Paul's resigned delivery (implied) and the specificity of 'asparagus' makes it funnier than a generic food joke would be. The dark sexual subtext is entirely in the audience's mind.

jokes.text: 'Where can I get the C train?' — Reverend Gimp asks after the wedding is called off
jokes.setup: The chaos of the ruined surprise wedding is playing out
jokes.punchline: The priest (whose name implies full leather fetish gear) is entirely practical about finding the subway — complete normality from someone with an absurd name/implied appearance
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the contrast: a person apparently dressed in full BDSM gear asking a completely mundane transit question. The name 'Reverend Gimp' does heavy lifting. The deadpan normality is the entire joke.

jokes.text: 'A-listers always have surprise weddings now, Liz. Timberbiel, Beyon-Z, Anne Hatha-nobody.'
jokes.setup: Jenna defends the concept of surprise weddings by citing celebrity examples
jokes.punchline: The celebrity name portmanteaus are deliberately bad puns, but 'Anne Hatha-nobody' is a withering insult disguised as a name joke — suggesting Anne Hathaway is a Z-lister
jokes.explanation: The escalating structure is key: 'Timberbiel' and 'Beyon-Z' are fun portmanteaus, but they set up 'Anne Hatha-nobody' as an actual celebrity putdown. The joke works on two levels — wordplay and shade — and 'Anne Hatha-nobody' became a quotable moment. Very Jenna.

jokes.text: 'technically, I am an A-lister now because I was on a list to date Tom Cruise, but I bailed before I got sucked in too deep, praise Xenu!'
jokes.setup: Jenna is justifying having an A-list surprise wedding
jokes.punchline: The Tom Cruise/Scientology joke is delivered with 'praise Xenu' — sincerely using Scientology's sacred term as a casual exclamation, implying she dodged a cult but absorbed its language
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'praise Xenu' as a throwaway sign-off is what elevates this. It implies Jenna got just close enough to Scientology to absorb some of it. Dark celebrity culture satire delivered with perfect Jenna obliviousness.

jokes.text: Cerie tells Liz 'It's inspiring to see that a woman in her 30s can still find true love.' Liz corrects her: 'I'm 42, Cerie.' Cerie responds: 'I don't know what that is.'
jokes.setup: Cerie offers what she thinks is a compliment
jokes.punchline: 'I don't know what that is' — Cerie doesn't understand the concept of being 42, existing in a world where such an age is outside her comprehension
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great two-step joke. The setup (Cerie thinks Liz is in her 30s) is already an insult, but the punchline — 'I don't know what that is' — is a perfectly calibrated Cerie moment. She's so young and bubble-brained that 42 is conceptually foreign to her. Perfect economy, perfect character voice.

jokes.text: The award description: 'Congratulations on being named one of the 80 Under 80, honoring women in entertainment who aren't Betty White!'
jokes.setup: Cerie announces Liz has won an award
jokes.punchline: The award category — 'under 80' and 'who aren't Betty White' — is a comically low bar that accidentally insults the recipient
jokes.explanation: The joke builds cleverly: 'Under 80' sounds oddly wide as a category, and 'who aren't Betty White' is the perfect absurdist exception that implies Betty White is in a class so transcendent she must be excluded. The backhanded honor Liz receives is perfectly calibrated to her character's self-esteem.

jokes.text: The ceremony will be broadcast on 'Lifetime... oh, dot com, backslash garbagefile'
jokes.setup: Cerie announces the ceremony will be on Lifetime — a real, prestigious network
jokes.punchline: The URL 'dot com backslash garbagefile' deflates the prestige completely and instantly
jokes.explanation: The pause before the deflating URL is a classic misdirection structure. 'garbagefile' is the perfect word — clinical, dismissive, and honest. Sharp comedy about digital media's hierarchy of prestige.

jokes.text: Liz does an excited dance/scat: 'Doo-ba-doo-ba-dow! Ba-doo-pomp-boo-pomp-boo-ba-da!'
jokes.setup: Liz is excited about winning an award
jokes.punchline: Instead of a normal reaction, she breaks into an improvised scat celebration — a visual/physical gag implying an awkward, dorky victory dance
jokes.explanation: Callbacks to joke #1 (Liz making up songs). The physical comedy of Liz's uncool celebration is entirely in the performance. Functional character moment but not a sharp written joke — depends heavily on Tina Fey's execution.

jokes.text: Liz attempts 'classic Girl Friday banter' with Jack: 'Now, you listen here, Jack. This story's not gonna write itself, see? / Oh, stop! You brute! I love you! Operator!'
jokes.setup: Liz wants to maintain their dynamic despite her being married
jokes.punchline: The 'banter' she demonstrates is a bizarre film noir mashup that makes no sense as a workplace dynamic — and she's doing both voices
jokes.explanation: Liz's attempt at 'banter' revealing she has no idea what real banter is, and the escalating absurdity of the film-noir snippets is a solid character joke. The specificity of 'Operator!' as a final non-sequitur lands well.

jokes.text: Jack's mother insists on traveling on Pearl Harbor Day 'to show the Emperor we're not afraid'
jokes.setup: Jack explains his mother arrives early for Christmas
jokes.punchline: She times her travel to Pearl Harbor Day as a geopolitical statement against Japan — decades late, entirely delusional, and framed with complete conviction
jokes.explanation: A wonderful character joke for Colleen — the patriotic delusion of an 87-year-old Irish-Catholic matriarch treating a December travel day as wartime defiance. 'The Emperor' as a casual reference is perfect period-accurate paranoia.

jokes.text: 'That's only 14 in demon years, Lemon. The woman's constant disapproval of me will keep her alive forever!'
jokes.setup: Liz says Jack should appreciate his mother who is 87
jokes.punchline: '14 in demon years' reframes the mother as a supernatural force; the second half explains the mechanism — her disapproval is life-sustaining
jokes.explanation: Two excellent jokes packed into one: first, the 'demon years' concept (like dog years but for demons) is completely original and perfectly characterizes Colleen. Second, the explanation that disapproval literally keeps her alive is both darkly funny and thematically resonant for the entire episode. Highly quotable, strong craft.

jokes.text: Jack's phone ring is described as 'shriller' for his mother, implying he has a specific ringtone for her shrill quality
jokes.setup: Jack identifies that his mother is calling
jokes.punchline: 'Notice the ring is shriller' — he's calibrated the ringtone to her personality
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional gag that characterizes Colleen economically. Not especially original but well-integrated into the scene.

jokes.text: Jack's assistant on the phone tells Colleen that Liz is with Jack: 'Well, she's wearing it pulled back, but it's not working. Exactly, because of her ears.'
jokes.setup: The assistant is relaying the call — we only hear one side
jokes.punchline: The conversation has immediately pivoted to critiquing Liz Lemon's hair and ears — Colleen's priorities on full display
jokes.explanation: The overheard half-conversation is a well-executed structural joke. The specificity of 'because of her ears' makes it funnier than a generic insult — Colleen has clearly thought about this. Good character establishment for both Colleen and her dismissal of Liz.

jokes.text: Kenneth explains why he's mopping the floor angrily: 'First Miss Lemon fired my girlfriend, and now Hazel broke up with me.' — the same person
jokes.setup: Tracy asks why Kenneth is mopping angrily
jokes.punchline: Kenneth lists two separate grievances that are the same event — revealing he doesn't understand that Hazel IS his girlfriend
jokes.explanation: A subtle but effective Kenneth joke — his emotional simplicity means he processes the same event as two separate injustices. Perfect character voice.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Because despite cell phones, iPads, and computers, it's still the most effective portal for poltergeists?'
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks Tracy if he knows why Kenneth loves TV
jokes.punchline: Tracy's guess is that TV is the best paranormal communication device — delivered with complete confidence as if this is established fact
jokes.explanation: A perfectly calibrated Tracy Jordan non-sequitur. The 'despite cell phones, iPads, and computers' framing is great — he's acknowledging modern technology only to dismiss it in favor of poltergeists. Only Tracy Jordan would say this.

jokes.text: 'The people you care about never leave. And the bad guy always gets what she deserves.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth explains what he loves about TV — that things don't change
jokes.punchline: The final line ('the bad guy always gets what she deserves') is clearly directed at Liz, who fired Hazel — Kenneth's idealized TV logic is revealed as a revenge fantasy
jokes.explanation: The specific pronoun 'she' doing all the work here — Kenneth's passive-aggression disguised as TV appreciation. A subtle but well-constructed moment.

jokes.text: Someone comments 'Someone's looking lovely today!' then adds: 'What a burn! I could have meant someone else. Although I didn't. She's radiant.'
jokes.setup: A compliment is offered to someone (implied to be Jenna stuffing her face in grief)
jokes.punchline: The immediate walk-back ('What a burn! I could have meant someone else') followed by confirmation makes the backhanded compliment a triple-layered insult
jokes.explanation: The self-aware commentary on the insult ('What a burn!') is a nice meta touch. Slightly undercut by unclear attribution, but the structure is solid.

jokes.text: Jenna, having found out her surprise wedding is ruined: 'Since I'm not getting married today, I might as well stuff my face.'
jokes.setup: Jenna's surprise wedding has been thwarted
jokes.punchline: Her response is immediate and purely appetite-driven — no grief, no anger, just pragmatic comfort eating
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat. The joke is in Jenna's immediate pivot from romantic devastation to food. Functional but not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: 'My whole life is thunder!'
jokes.setup: Liz tries to apologize: 'I didn't mean to steal your thunder'
jokes.punchline: 'My whole life is thunder!' — a completely unhinged self-aggrandizing response that reframes Jenna's entire existence as dramatic spectacle
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best single-line jokes in the series. It takes the idiom 'steal your thunder' and Jenna reframes it cosmically — she IS the thunder, all of it, always. The perfect distillation of her character in four words. Maximum economy, maximum character specificity, highly quotable. This is what a 9+ looks like.

jokes.text: 'Next you'll tell me Mickey Rourke catapulted you into the Hollywood sign!'
jokes.setup: Jenna is escalating her grievances about Liz's life achievements
jokes.punchline: A completely non-sequitur scenario involving Mickey Rourke and a catapult — Jenna's spiral of paranoid imagination conjures the most specific and bizarre threat possible
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Mickey Rourke (not a generic celebrity — someone with the right energy for deranged physical stunts) and 'catapulted' as the verb of choice makes this a genuinely inventive absurdist escalation. Jenna's grievance list reaching this level of surreal specificity is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: 'did you know that Chuck Scarborough is anatomically a woman? So I am a lesbian.'
jokes.setup: Liz is talking up the prestige of the award by listing past recipients
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Chuck Scarborough (a male NYC news anchor) is 'anatomically a woman' and Liz's immediate logical leap to 'so I am a lesbian' is a perfect absurdist non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: A classic 30 Rock rapid-fire non-sequitur that makes perfect internal logic while being completely absurd. The immediate 'so I am a lesbian' shows Liz's brain working through implications in real time. The specific name 'Chuck Scarborough' adds to the joke.

jokes.text: Liz's flashback/fantasy of first meeting Jenna: Jenna in period costume ('What brings a mummer to Lightsman's Row?') speaking to a young boy — revealed to be Liz
jokes.setup: Liz is reminiscing about meeting Jenna 15 years ago in the lighting world in Chicago
jokes.punchline: The flashback is rendered in an absurdly theatrical/period style, with Jenna in costume and Liz apparently presenting as a young boy
jokes.explanation: 30 Rock's stylized flashback format — making the past look like a period drama — is reliably funny. 'What brings a mummer to Lightsman's Row?' as Jenna's casual greeting is absurdly theatrical. The visual of Liz as a small boy is a good visual gag.

jokes.text: 'Oh, Liz, you had me at "Hayden Panettiere is dead"!'
jokes.setup: Liz asks Jenna to appear on stage with her at the award ceremony, promising cameras will be there
jokes.punchline: Jenna agrees — but her 'you had me at...' romantic-comedy moment is triggered by the fake celebrity death, not any heartfelt sentiment
jokes.explanation: Subverts the 'You had me at hello' romantic trope with a dark celebrity death fake-out. The specificity of Hayden Panettiere (Heroes actress, contemporary, someone Jenna would see as competition) makes it feel targeted rather than random. Perfect Jenna — cameras + rival's death = agreement. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: A woman approaches Jack: 'I'm a nymphomaniac virgin widow, and I just completed my year of mourning. And I've got a hotel room and a latex allergy, and I was just wondering what you were doing for the next 12 to 14 hours.'
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to do 'absolutely nothing' to avoid his mother's disapproval
jokes.punchline: A woman with an escalating list of contradictory/absurd qualifications approaches with a very specific sexual proposition — each new detail is funnier than the last
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly structured escalating list joke. 'Nymphomaniac virgin widow' is already a paradox of three, then 'latex allergy' adds specificity, and '12 to 14 hours' is the deadpan precision that brings it home. The escalation is pitch-perfect. One of the episode's stronger written jokes.

jokes.text: Colleen appears just as Jack is about to leave with the woman: 'Nice try, Mother.' — implying Colleen staged the entire encounter
jokes.setup: Jack was about to escape with the nymphomaniac widow
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Colleen orchestrated the temptation to catch Jack doing something disapproved-of is a perfect escalation of her supernatural scheming
jokes.explanation: The reveal recontextualizes the entire previous scene as a Colleen honeytrap. The implication that Colleen found and briefed a nymphomaniac virgin widow specifically to catch Jack is gloriously absurd. 'Your powers remain strong, old one' elevates the callback.

jokes.text: Colleen: 'The Grim Reaper, who is black, I assume, what, with the hoodies he wears.'
jokes.setup: Colleen says she wants to talk to Jack before she 'meets the Grim Reaper'
jokes.punchline: She speculates the Grim Reaper is Black based on hoodie fashion — a period-specific, racist, and completely oblivious comment that characterizes Colleen as an unreconstructed bigot
jokes.explanation: A sharp satirical joke that works because it's clearly satirizing Colleen's casual racism rather than endorsing it. The reference to hoodie fashion (a contemporary 2012 Trayvon Martin-era reference) makes it pointed social commentary through character. The obliviousness is key to the comedy.

jokes.text: Jack recites Colleen's 'dying speech' from memory: 'How could you do this to me? You're such a huge disappointment. If only Dragnet hadn't been preempted because of Sputnik, you never would have been conceived!'
jokes.setup: Jack claims he has his mother's dying speech memorized from all her previous false alarms
jokes.punchline: The speech is a perfect escalating guilt trip culminating in 'you never would have been conceived' — blaming a TV preemption for Jack's existence
jokes.explanation: An exceptionally well-constructed joke. The premise (Jack knows the dying speech by heart) is already funny, but the speech itself is a masterpiece of escalating passive aggression — ending with the implication that Sputnik pre-empting Dragnet led directly to Jack's conception, which is framed as a tragedy. The specificity of 'Sputnik' and 'Dragnet' is perfect historical detail. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Re: the scout master: 'I didn't trust that scout master. He was always wearing shorts.'
jokes.setup: Jack mentions Colleen faked a heart attack to keep him from going camping
jokes.punchline: Her justification — shorts are suspicious — is delivered as if this is perfectly reasonable logic
jokes.explanation: A classic 30 Rock economy joke. 'He was always wearing shorts' as the full extent of a suspicious person's suspicious behavior is perfect deadpan Colleen logic — priggish, era-specific, and completely absurd.

jokes.text: Tracy reveals he had the mice spell out 'Come see me' in crumbs on the floor
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks why there are crumbs on the floor he was mopping
jokes.punchline: Tracy trained (or arranged) mice to spell words in crumbs as a communication method
jokes.explanation: Only Tracy Jordan would use mice as a messaging system. The matter-of-fact explanation ('Yes, Kenneth') makes it funnier. The visual of mice spelling words is a great 30 Rock absurdist visual gag that only works in single-camera.

jokes.text: Florence Henderson appears as 'special guest star' — Tracy says 'None of that Brady stuff' and she immediately asks: 'Are you the perverts who want to go to town on each other while I make a pie?'
jokes.setup: Tracy has arranged for Florence Henderson to appear for Kenneth's benefit
jokes.punchline: Florence Henderson — TV's quintessential wholesome mother — arrives expecting a perverted booking and frames it as just another job
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: it subverts Florence Henderson's wholesome image, implies she has done this before ('which booking is this?'), and the specific detail of 'making a pie' while something perverted happens is a perfect dark absurdist touch. One of the episode's best gags — takes a celebrity cameo and makes it genuinely funny rather than stunt-casting.

jokes.text: Awards MC Bonny Badamath: 'I can't shake hands because I have carpal tunnel syndrome from zipping up my own dress now that Gary's gone.'
jokes.setup: The awards ceremony MC introduces herself
jokes.punchline: Oversharing her carpal tunnel's cause — the specific, pathetic detail of being unable to zip her own dress, tied to Gary's absence — turns a formal introduction into a sad character portrait
jokes.explanation: A masterfully efficient piece of character comedy — in one sentence, we know Bonny is recently widowed/divorced, lonely, and overshares. 'Now that Gary's gone' does enormous sad-funny work. The carpal tunnel as physical consequence of loneliness is darkly clever.

jokes.text: Bonny: 'Well, I'm just glad you found the place, what, with my directions. Because Gary was the navigator.'
jokes.setup: Bonny is greeting Liz at the ceremony
jokes.punchline: Another Gary reference — 'Gary was the navigator' extends the character joke of Bonny's life having collapsed without Gary
jokes.explanation: A callback to the Gary joke that works as a running gag about Bonny's Gary-shaped hole. Slightly weaker than the original because the pattern is now established, but the specificity of 'navigator' is good.

jokes.text: Liz sees her photo in the program: 'Why does the other Liz Lemon always come up first?' — implying there's a more famous Liz Lemon whose Google results crowd her out
jokes.setup: Liz is excited to see her picture in the event program
jokes.punchline: The photo was pulled from the internet, but a different Liz Lemon comes up first in searches — a perfect deflation of Liz's ego at her own award ceremony
jokes.explanation: A smart joke about internet identity and obscurity. The fact that Liz Lemon — a fictional character, famous within her world — is not the top result for her own name is both relatable and perfectly calibrated to her status as a semi-famous person. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Liz discovers Jenna is setting up her own wedding in the ceremony venue to ruin Liz's award moment
jokes.setup: Liz comes back to find the venue being rearranged
jokes.punchline: Jenna has mobilized wedding infrastructure during the bathroom break to stage a counter-event — the audacity and speed of the sabotage is the joke
jokes.explanation: A well-structured escalation of the Jenna revenge plot. The callback to the surprise wedding setup (joke #3) pays off here. Liz's 'My best friend' delivered as a flat reaction beat is a great deadpan moment.

jokes.text: A woman at the ceremony empathizes with Liz's best friend problems: 'You know what my best friend did for my 50th birthday? She gives everybody a car. And then she was all, "Thank you for coming to Gayle's birthday!"'
jokes.setup: A woman is sharing a story about a self-centered best friend
jokes.punchline: The story is clearly about Oprah (giving away cars, Gayle's birthday) but delivered from the perspective of someone who resents it — the punchline is the revelation of who these 'best friends' are
jokes.explanation: A clever misdirection — we're drawn into a relatable venting session about a narcissistic friend before realizing the speaker is Gayle King and the 'best friend' is Oprah. The joke reframes Oprah's famous generosity as social one-upmanship from her best friend's perspective.

jokes.text: Gayle King explains her best friend grievance: 'When I got bangs, my best friend didn't even acknowledge them... after reading an article in my best friend's magazine, I realized my feelings are valid.'
jokes.setup: Gayle is listing Oprah's failures as a best friend
jokes.punchline: She validated her feelings about Oprah by reading Oprah's magazine — the total Oprah ecosystem means even her grievances are mediated through Oprah content
jokes.explanation: The structural irony is excellent: Gayle reads Oprah's magazine to validate her feelings about Oprah. The detail about bangs is great because it's such a small, specific grievance to have against someone as omnipresent as Oprah. 'My best friend's magazine' doing double duty as possessive and product reference.

jokes.text: When I got bangs, my best friend didn't even acknowledge them. So I was gonna grow them out. Then, after reading an article in my best friend's magazine, I realized my feelings are valid. So I had to say to her, 'My bangs, they're not about you. It's about me trying to cover my forehead.'
jokes.setup: Liz is commiserating about difficult best friends, making what she thinks is an anonymous complaint.
jokes.punchline: Every detail of Liz's 'complaint' references Oprah — the magazine (O Magazine), the best friend not acknowledging her bangs (Gayle). Liz doesn't realize she's talking about Oprah to Oprah.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Liz is obliviously criticizing Oprah to Oprah's face. 'My best friend's magazine' as a reference to O Magazine is a clever escalation. The payoff — 'We're talking about Oprah, right? / No, of course not. / She can hear us!' — is a perfect three-beat closer. Strong structure.

jokes.text: 'We're talking about Oprah, right? / No, of course not. She can hear us!'
jokes.setup: Liz has figured out who they're talking about
jokes.punchline: Gayle's fearful 'She can hear us!' confirms it's Oprah while also treating her as an omniscient supernatural force
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Oprah-as-god running theme. 'She can hear us!' is perfectly paranoid and implies Oprah has surveillance capabilities. Great economy — three words do enormous work.

jokes.text: Colleen's dying preparations: 'These are the clothes that I want to be buried in. And make sure I'm holding this. Glue the pin to the inside of the coffin lid.' / 'For grave robbers.'
jokes.setup: Colleen is giving Jack her dying instructions
jokes.punchline: She has elaborate anti-grave-robber countermeasures built into her funeral planning
jokes.explanation: Colleen's paranoia about grave robbers as a serious consideration in her funeral planning is a wonderfully specific character detail. The pin on the inside of the coffin lid suggests she intends to fight back from within.

jokes.text: 'I went down to a pack a day for you!' — Colleen justifying her sacrifices as a mother
jokes.setup: Colleen is lecturing Jack about not being appreciative
jokes.punchline: Reducing her smoking from a presumably higher number to 'a pack a day' is framed as a maternal sacrifice
jokes.explanation: Perfect Colleen character economy. The implication that she was previously smoking more than a pack a day as a baseline, and cutting to 'only' a pack counts as a parental sacrifice, is a rich character detail. Classic 30 Rock one-liner.

jokes.text: Colleen's stroke symptoms: 'I was watching TV, and they started interviewing an Asian Santa Claus, and my arm went numb!'
jokes.setup: Jack asks what happened to trigger the health scare
jokes.punchline: Colleen's stroke was apparently triggered by the offense of an Asian Santa Claus on television
jokes.explanation: A sharp satirical joke — Colleen's racism literally gives her a stroke. The writing has it both ways: it's funny and a pointed critique of people who have actual physical stress responses to diversity. The specificity ('Asian Santa Claus' rather than any other race) and the psychosomatic medical detail make this exceptional.

jokes.text: 'My father did not kill dozens of Germans so that his daughter could die in a van!'
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to get Colleen to call an ambulance
jokes.punchline: Refusing an ambulance because of WWII service — the non-sequitur logic of honoring her father's sacrifice through transportation choices is perfectly absurd Colleen reasoning
jokes.explanation: The rhetorical logic is impeccable nonsense — WWII sacrifice creates an entitlement to die somewhere other than an ambulance van. 'Dozens of Germans' is the perfect specific number (not hundreds, not scores — dozens). Highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'But he wasn't even in the war!' — Jack's deflation of the heroic narrative
jokes.setup: Colleen invokes her father's WWII heroism
jokes.punchline: Jack's flat correction: the father wasn't even in the war — the entire mythology is invented
jokes.explanation: A perfect deflating punchline. The economy is superb — seven words that demolish Colleen's entire rhetorical edifice. The gap between her grandiose WWII narrative and the reality is the whole joke.

jokes.text: Colleen: 'Just leave the door open, and let the elements take me.' — her preferred method of death
jokes.setup: Colleen insists she doesn't want medical help
jokes.punchline: She'd rather die by passive exposure to 'the elements' — a theatrical but weirdly dignified exit plan
jokes.explanation: Colleen's theatrical death wish delivered as a practical suggestion. 'The elements' as a New York City apartment option is quietly funny — what elements, exactly?

jokes.text: Colleen: 'I'll take a horse-drawn carriage.' Jack: 'Those carriages are rolling torture wagons for nature's most dignified creature! The horse is one of only three appropriate subjects for a painting, along with ships with sails and men holding up swords while staring off into the distance.'
jokes.setup: Colleen insists on a horse-drawn carriage to the hospital
jokes.punchline: Jack's defense of horses becomes an elaborate aesthetic manifesto about the only three valid subjects for painting — a completely unprompted declaration of WASP art theory
jokes.explanation: A great character joke for Jack. His passion for horses escalates into an absurdist aesthetic theory ('nature's most dignified creature') and then a confident declaration of what constitutes valid art. 'Men holding up swords while staring off into the distance' is the perfect specific third item that reveals Jack's patrician worldview. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'I'm going out of this world exactly the way I came into it. Wearing a hat!'
jokes.setup: Colleen declares she will die on her own terms
jokes.punchline: The grand declaration of dying as she was born collapses into 'wearing a hat' — an absurdly specific and un-dramatic birth detail
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: grand rhetorical build ('exactly the way I came into it') with a supremely deflating punchline. The misdirection leads us to expect something profound or bawdy — instead it's a hat. The specificity of having been born wearing a hat implies she came into the world with pretension pre-installed. Exceptional economy and structure.

jokes.text: Tracy asks Kenneth if the sun-bleached janitor is 'the same guy as before, or does that sun-bleached turd have a twin brother?'
jokes.setup: Tracy approaches an elevator
jokes.punchline: 'Sun-bleached turd' as a description of a pale/sun-damaged person — delivered with genuine inquiry rather than malice
jokes.explanation: Tracy insult comedy — vivid but not particularly structured. 'Sun-bleached turd' is a memorable image but the joke is essentially just a colorful insult with a functional setup.

jokes.text: Tracy's elevator plan backfires: 'This was a bad idea! Is this alcohol-based? Why are you doing this to me, Jacob?!'
jokes.setup: Tracy gets trapped in the elevator he planned to use to teach Kenneth a lesson
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately panics, asks if a hand sanitizer is alcohol-based, and calls out to 'Jacob' — a completely unknown person — as his panic escalates
jokes.explanation: Tracy's instant self-betrayal of his own scheme is great character comedy. The non-sequitur 'Why are you doing this to me, Jacob?!' invoking an unknown person is a perfect Tracy spiral. The alcohol question implies he needs a drink immediately.

jokes.text: Awards MC: 'I am told she got married just today. Just like Gary and that bitch who was selling us our dream house.'
jokes.setup: Bonny is introducing Liz at the awards ceremony
jokes.punchline: Another Gary overshare — and this one reveals that Gary left Bonny for someone he met while they were house-shopping
jokes.explanation: The best of the Bonny/Gary running gag. The specific detail of 'the bitch who was selling us our dream house' gives the Gary backstory maximum tragicomic impact. It's both funny and genuinely sad — and Bonny is saying this into a microphone at a formal event.

jokes.text: The DVD/disc fails to play at the ceremony: 'Hang on. This is being weird. / Blow on the disc. / Is it on the right component? / Try unplugging it and plugging it back in! / Just open the disc part and blow on it!'
jokes.setup: The awards ceremony is trying to show a clip of Liz's work
jokes.punchline: The tech failure at a formal ceremony — with everyone offering their specific folk remedy — is a recognizable cringe comedy beat about AV incompetence at events
jokes.explanation: A recognizable observational joke about AV failures at events. The specific suggestion of blowing on the disc (a video game cartridge trick) is the sharpest detail. Functional but not especially crafted — could be in almost any show.

jokes.text: Jenna emerges holding the disc: 'Looking for this?' — villain reveal
jokes.setup: The ceremony can't find why the disc won't play
jokes.punchline: Jenna has stolen the disc as sabotage — the villain reveal is both dramatically satisfying and funny because of her commitment
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the secret plan setup. Jenna's delivery as a cartoonish villain — presenting the disc dramatically — is the joke. Good structure, entirely character-dependent.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'Without me, you'd still be behind that light board in Chicago turning bags of Sour Patch Kids inside out to lick them clean.' Liz: 'I got my money's worth!'
jokes.setup: Jenna taunts Liz with where she'd be without her help
jokes.punchline: The image is specific and degrading (turning Sour Patch Kids bags inside out to lick them), and Liz's proud defense of this practice is the kill shot
jokes.explanation: Excellent two-part joke. Jenna's insult contains a perfectly specific detail (Sour Patch Kids, turned inside out, licked clean) that captures exactly the kind of pathetic frugality appropriate to Liz Lemon in her Chicago days. Then Liz's defensive 'I got my money's worth!' completely owns the image and makes it funnier — she's not embarrassed, she's proud. The synergy between setup and response is exceptional.

jokes.text: 'And without me, you'd still be doing local commercials for store-brand douches. / Well, joke's on you because that wasn't a commercial. I don't know what it was!'
jokes.setup: Liz and Jenna are trading origin-story insults
jokes.punchline: Jenna's defense of the store-brand douche work — 'that wasn't a commercial. I don't know what it was!' — admits something worse happened while refusing to elaborate
jokes.explanation: A masterful two-step joke. Liz's insult about the douche commercial is funny, but Jenna's response is funnier — by saying 'that wasn't a commercial, I don't know what it was,' she implies something far more degrading occurred while protecting herself through ignorance. The denial-as-confession structure is excellent.

jokes.text: 'I swear to God, you are the most selfish human being on the planet. / Thank you. Visit my website for extras and ringtones.'
jokes.setup: Liz calls out Jenna's selfishness
jokes.punchline: Jenna accepts the insult as a compliment and pivots to a website plug — treating 'most selfish human being' as a brand identity
jokes.explanation: The pivot from insult to brand promotion is perfectly Jenna. 'Visit my website for extras and ringtones' in the middle of a screaming confrontation is an absurdist non-sequitur that also completely defines her character — she's monetizing her selfishness in real time. One of the episode's best character moments.

jokes.text: I swear to God, you are the most selfish human being on the planet. Thank you. Visit my website for extras and ringtones.
jokes.setup: Liz accuses Jenna of being the most selfish person on earth.
jokes.punchline: Jenna takes it as a compliment and immediately pivots to brand promotion — 'visit my website for extras and ringtones' — as if Liz has just praised her brand.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect character joke. Jenna receives an insult, treats it as PR, and immediately activates brand-promotion mode. 'Visit my website for extras and ringtones' sounds like a circa-2012 celebrity website plug and is hilarious for its dated specificity. The unselfconsciousness of Jenna's pivot is the entire joke. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jenna bribes the lighting tech to light the stage 'like a grocery store milk aisle'
jokes.setup: Jenna wants to sabotage Liz's appearance on stage
jokes.punchline: 'Lit like a grocery store milk aisle' — a perfectly specific description of the most unflattering, harshest, most institutional lighting possible
jokes.explanation: An inspired specific image. 'Grocery store milk aisle' is the perfect comedic choice — everyone knows the specific horror of that institutional fluorescent lighting, and using lighting expertise (which both Liz and Jenna's origin story involves) as the weapon is beautifully character-integrated.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'Also, you need to tell your Aunt Mary, when she was two, there was an accident with a hot comb. And, well, she used to be a boy.'
jokes.setup: Colleen is giving Jack her final confessions before death
jokes.punchline: The most dramatic deathbed secret — a family member's gender history — delivered as a casual addendum, with the cause being a mundane hot comb accident
jokes.explanation: A dark secrets joke in the Colleen tradition. The casual delivery of a life-changing revelation is the joke — Colleen frames the hot comb accident and gender transformation as equivalent footnotes. The absurdist causal logic (hot comb > gender change) is very 30 Rock.

jokes.text: Jack challenges Colleen's apparent change of heart: 'Since when did you ever care about happiness?' / 'Don't talk to me like that, Jack! I breastfed you for nine years!'
jokes.setup: Colleen claims she just wants Jack to be happy
jokes.punchline: Colleen's defense of her parenting credentials is nine years of breastfeeding — an absurdly long period that functions as both a sacrifice and a guilt weapon
jokes.explanation: Nine years of breastfeeding is an absurd escalation of the sacrifice concept, and it perfectly characterizes Colleen — she weaponizes her most intimate maternal act as a debate-stopper. The specificity of 'nine years' (not 'a long time') makes it funnier. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Paul, inside the steamer trunk for hours: 'It's all right! The lack of oxygen is making me orgasm!'
jokes.setup: Liz confronts Jenna about Paul being trapped in a steamer trunk
jokes.punchline: Paul's muffled reassurance from inside the trunk is that the oxygen deprivation has a sexual benefit — completely calm, entirely in character
jokes.explanation: Perfect Paul moment. His character is defined by cheerful acceptance of extreme situations, and autoerotic asphyxiation as a happy accident while trapped in a trunk is both dark and entirely in character. The muffled delivery from inside the trunk makes it funnier as a visual gag.

jokes.text: Judy (a random audience member) defends Jenna: 'We shouldn't be defining ourselves by our men.' / Jenna: 'Oh, so in order to be independent, we have to be asexual? / You would know, Judy!'
jokes.setup: A random award ceremony attendee weighs in on the Liz/Jenna confrontation
jokes.punchline: 'You would know, Judy!' — Jenna deploys Judy's apparent asexuality as a put-down with no setup for who Judy even is
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the complete unexplained specificity of 'You would know, Judy' — we know nothing about Judy except that Jenna has apparently diagnosed her asexuality. The throwaway character insult is a functional quick laugh.

jokes.text: Bonny: 'God, I miss Gary so much! I put his sweater on a body pillow... I took it for a canoe ride!'
jokes.setup: The award ceremony has devolved into chaos
jokes.punchline: Bonny inserts her Gary grief with a physical escalation — the sweater-on-body-pillow is relatable pathetic, but taking it for a canoe ride is the perfect absurdist escalation
jokes.explanation: The perfect payoff of the Bonny/Gary running gag. The two-beat structure is excellent: 'I put his sweater on a body pillow' lands as sad-funny, then 'I took it for a canoe ride' is the escalating absurdist detail that makes the whole thing. The canoe ride is brilliantly specific — intimate, romantic, and completely deranged. One of the episode's best running-gag payoffs.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Fire up the Lekos! And the Klieg!' — deploying theatrical lighting knowledge as a weapon against Jenna's sabotage
jokes.setup: Jenna has weaponized the stage lighting against Liz
jokes.punchline: Liz calls out specific theatrical lighting equipment (Lekos, Klieg lights) — using her long-forgotten lighting board background against Jenna
jokes.explanation: A callback to the 15-years-ago lighting board origin story. The joke is that Liz — usually defined by her writing career — turns out to have retained her lighting expertise specifically for this confrontation. The specific technical terms (Lekos, Klieg) reward attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Liz deflates Colleen's apparent last words: 'Really? 'Cause that doesn't sound like her, but I guess people do say strange things at the end. My grandmother said, "Liz, stop playing with the flesh around my elbow."'
jokes.setup: Jack shares that Colleen said she just wants him to be happy
jokes.punchline: Liz's grandmother's final words were a request to stop playing with elbow skin — a grotesque, mundane, and specific final request that is the opposite of profound
jokes.explanation: An exceptional Liz Lemon character joke. 'Stop playing with the flesh around my elbow' is the perfect grotesque detail — both deeply specific (why the elbow?) and completely unpoetic as final words. It also characterizes young Liz as someone who would do exactly that at a deathbed. One of the episode's best individual lines.

jokes.text: Jack reframes Colleen's 'I just want you to be happy' as the most devastating insult: 'You say it to someone who has disappointed you.'
jokes.setup: Liz insists the dying words were sweet
jokes.punchline: Jack's analysis that 'I just want you to be happy' = the ultimate expression of lowered expectations is both funny and emotionally true
jokes.explanation: A brilliant inversion that works on multiple levels. Jack's analysis — that 'be happy' is the phrase you use when you've given up on someone achieving anything — is genuinely insightful AND devastating AND funny. It completes the theme of Colleen's disapproval while giving Jack a final gift from her. One of the episode's most sophisticated jokes.

jokes.text: 'No. It's perfect. She's a genius. One last twist of the knife.'
jokes.setup: Jack processes Colleen's final message
jokes.punchline: He celebrates his mother's posthumous psychological manipulation as genius — with genuine admiration rather than grief
jokes.explanation: Jack's proud admiration for his mother's final act of cruelty is the perfect Jack Donaghy response to Colleen's death. 'She's a genius' applied to posthumous psychological warfare is darkly funny and entirely in character. The warmth in his appreciation makes it sweeter and sadder.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Colleen wanted to be buried before the rest of the family found out and sold her body to a haunted house.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains the funeral timeline
jokes.punchline: The Donaghy family's anticipated response to Colleen's death is to monetize her corpse via seasonal entertainment
jokes.explanation: A superb dark comedy line that establishes the Donaghy family as both mercenary and seasonally opportunistic. The specificity of 'haunted house' (not a medical school, not a funeral home — a Halloween attraction) is perfect. One of the episode's most quotable moments.

jokes.text: Jack: 'One more chance to disappoint her as she looks up at me from her throne in Hell.'
jokes.setup: Jack must write Colleen's eulogy
jokes.punchline: 'Her throne in Hell' — Colleen is not in Heaven but reigning in Hell, and 'looking up' means she'll be watching the eulogy from below
jokes.explanation: The 'throne in Hell' establishes Colleen's spiritual destination while honoring her power — she's not just in Hell, she's REIGNING there. 'Looking up at me' is the clever pivot: technically 'looking up' from Hell, while the phrase usually implies admiration. Perfect double meaning.

jokes.text: Jenna's rare emotional honesty: 'All these years, I've always been able to look at you and feel better about myself.' / Liz: 'Sure.' / 'Don't interrupt.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is opening up emotionally to Liz
jokes.punchline: Her heartfelt opening is that looking at Liz makes her feel better about herself — and when Liz complacently agrees, Jenna reprimands the interruption
jokes.explanation: A well-structured joke built on Jenna's character — her 'vulnerability' is actually a backhanded insult, and her 'Don't interrupt' when Liz meekly agrees shows Jenna can't even have a confessional without controlling it.

jokes.text: 'The pill that lets me feel emotion is gonna wear off soon.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is in an uncharacteristically sincere emotional moment
jokes.punchline: She's only having feelings because of a pharmaceutical — implying she takes medication specifically to be able to experience emotions, and is monitoring its depletion
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent character joke. The implication that Jenna requires medication to experience basic human emotions — and is aware of and managing this — is the perfect distillation of her as a character. 'The pill that lets me feel emotion' is superb economy. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jenna's emotional confessional spirals into: 'you're married to a guy that I think about during sex.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is cataloging the ways Liz's life improvements have upset her equilibrium
jokes.punchline: Among Liz's offenses: her husband is Jenna's sexual fantasy — framed as a grievance rather than a compliment
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Jenna frames a compliment about Criss as a personal affront. That she experiences this as a Liz-inflicted injury rather than acknowledging the awkwardness is perfectly Jenna.

jokes.text: Watching you struggle at work, dating losers, wearing boys' husky jeans -- / They have reinforced crotches.
jokes.setup: Jenna is cataloguing the things she used to use to make herself feel better about her life.
jokes.punchline: The boys' husky jeans get a defense from Liz: 'They have reinforced crotches.' She's not embarrassed — she's sold on the practical benefits.
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely Liz's defense — not 'they're comfortable' or even 'they fit' but 'they have reinforced crotches,' a structural/technical argument for children's husky jeans. Her complete lack of shame and the specificity of the defense is peak Liz. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: The pill wears off: 'Pill wearing off. You have mom arms.'
jokes.setup: Jenna just delivered a heartfelt reconciliation speech
jokes.punchline: The emotion evaporates on cue and she immediately reverts to physical criticism — 'mom arms' as the first thought when the feeling filter drops
jokes.explanation: The perfect callback payoff to joke #68. The structure is flawless: the emotional pill wears off mid-scene with a clinical announcement, and the first thing Jenna notices without the emotional filter is Liz's arm situation. 'Mom arms' is the most Jenna possible thought. The timing — immediately after a heartfelt moment — makes the laugh enormous. One of the episode's top two jokes alongside 'My whole life is thunder.'

jokes.text: Tracy presents 'Hazel' but it's a different actress: 'I recast her! She tested through the roof! / At the STD clinic.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth is told Hazel is back
jokes.punchline: Tracy has literally recast the role of Kenneth's girlfriend with a different actress — treating real life like a TV production — and the 'tested through the roof' has a double meaning revealed by 'at the STD clinic'
jokes.explanation: Brilliant execution of the episode's TV-life-blur theme. Tracy's solution to Hazel leaving Kenneth is to recast her — and the 'tested through the roof / at the STD clinic' double meaning is a perfectly structured two-line joke. The meta-commentary on TV logic applied to real life is excellent.

jokes.text: Tracy's speech: 'Where else but real life would a millionaire movie star care so much about a hillbilly janitor that he would spend two days trying to cheer him up? You can't do that on television because if you did, no one would watch.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is explaining why real life is better than TV
jokes.punchline: His evidence for real life's superiority is their relationship — but he immediately undermines it by acknowledging that their dynamic is too implausible to be on TV
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever meta-joke. Tracy proves real life is better than TV by noting that real life contains scenarios too implausible for TV — while being in a TV show. The 'no one would watch' self-deprecation from a character on a TV show is a sophisticated fourth-wall graze. Good structure.

jokes.text: 'I sure picked the right week to come back. / You weren't supposed to have any lines, Quon Lee. Now I have to pay you!'
jokes.setup: A background character makes a comment about the dramatic week
jokes.punchline: Tracy breaks the fiction by complaining he now has to pay this person as a speaking actor — a meta-joke about TV production contracts
jokes.explanation: A sharp meta-joke about SAG/AFTRA rules regarding background actors gaining speaking roles. Tracy's awareness of production economics — and his annoyance that he now owes Quon Lee — is a great instance of 30 Rock's meta-referential style.

jokes.text: Jack: 'The man who in 1984 wore a tuxedo so well, he broke up the Go-Go's.'
jokes.setup: Jack is establishing his credentials in the eulogy
jokes.punchline: The causal connection between wearing a tuxedo well and breaking up the Go-Go's is a perfectly absurdist piece of Jack mythology
jokes.explanation: A beautiful absurdist boast. The Go-Go's break-up as a consequence of Jack's sartorial excellence is exactly the kind of delusional self-mythology Jack Donaghy would have. The year 1984 is perfect — specific enough to feel real, and the Go-Go's broke up around that time. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: The eulogy begins: 'Dublin. 1852. A ship bobs in the lee tide of the icy Irish Sea. Her name? Ariel.'
jokes.setup: Jack has promised 'the greatest eulogy of all time'
jokes.punchline: The eulogy opens like a Homeric epic — set in Dublin, 1852, following a ship named Ariel — for what is presumably a funeral in modern New York
jokes.explanation: The joke is the scope — Jack's eulogy starts 160 years before Colleen's birth in a different country. The epic style ('bobs in the lee tide') applied to an Irish immigrant origin story played with complete seriousness is well-executed character comedy.

jokes.text: Eulogizing montage: 'Today we are all Irish! / And the plumber says, "I don't-a know, but that's a pretty big-a pizza!" / Life is for the living!'
jokes.setup: Jack's eulogy has been going on for an indeterminate time
jokes.punchline: The scattered excerpts we hear include a JFK parody ('Today we are all Irish'), the punchline to a completely unrelated Italian plumber joke, and an aphorism — suggesting the eulogy has gone completely off the rails
jokes.explanation: The glimpses of the eulogy are constructed perfectly — the JFK parody is grandiose, then we get the punchline of an Italian joke with no setup (implying Jack has been telling a full joke during the eulogy), then a platitude. The cumulative absurdity of what 'the greatest eulogy of all time' actually contains is excellent.

jokes.text: 'Thank you, Kermit, for explaining the afterlife to us.' — apparently Kermit the Frog has been part of the eulogy
jokes.setup: The eulogy continues in ways we cannot see
jokes.punchline: Kermit the Frog has been brought in to explain the afterlife — a completely left-field guest whose appearance is taken in stride by the attendees
jokes.explanation: The shock of Kermit at a funeral being thanked for theological explanation is a magnificent absurdist gag. The mundane 'thank you, Kermit' suggests this is a normal eulogy occurrence. One of the episode's funniest conceits — we never see it, only hear the reaction, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Sir Paul McCartney and the Harlem Boys Choir perform at the funeral
jokes.setup: The eulogy has already featured Kermit the Frog
jokes.punchline: Sir Paul McCartney AND the Harlem Boys Choir are part of Colleen's funeral entertainment — the escalating celebrity roster for an Irish Catholic grandmother's funeral is the joke
jokes.explanation: Kermit + Paul McCartney + Harlem Boys Choir as a funeral trifecta is classic Jack Donaghy overreach. The combination is absurdly random yet specific enough to feel like Jack's aesthetic choices. Good escalation from the Kermit reveal.

jokes.text: Jenna's wedding vow: 'I promise not to make fun of you when you ask where your glasses are and they're on your head.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is reciting wedding vows
jokes.punchline: Her vow is to not mock a specific foible — implying she currently does mock it — framed as a generous promise
jokes.explanation: A vow that characterizes the relationship — Jenna must specifically promise not to mock Paul's most minor foibles, suggesting she's mocked everything else. 'They're on your head' is a good specific detail. Functional character joke.

jokes.text: Paul's wedding vow: 'I promise to always pour antibiotics all over your penis before you staple it to anything.'
jokes.setup: Paul is reading his vows to Jenna
jokes.punchline: The vow reveals a recurring activity requiring antibiotic preparation before penile stapling — delivered as a tender commitment
jokes.explanation: An exceptional dark comedy vow. The specificity of the act (stapling + antibiotics, not any other combination) and the caring intent (the antibiotics show concern for safety) delivered as a romantic vow is genuinely inventive. Paul's cheerful kinkiness getting a formal vow is perfect character work. One of the episode's standout jokes.

jokes.text: 'Ladies and gentlemen, presenting Mrs. and Mr. Jenna Maroneys!'
jokes.setup: The wedding officiant makes the traditional introduction
jokes.punchline: Paul has taken Jenna's surname — so they are both 'Jenna Maroneys' — and the 'Mrs. and Mr.' inverted order acknowledges who is actually in charge
jokes.explanation: A perfect closing joke. 'Mr. Jenna Maroneys' is the logical conclusion of everything we know about Paul and Jenna's dynamic — he exists to serve her brand. The plural of her name ('Maroneys') is a small but excellent additional absurdist detail. Great final beat.

tmdb_overview: Jenna annoys Liz with her wedding envy, Jack devises a plan to avoid disappointing his visiting mother and Tracy attempts to cheer up Kenneth.
insight: Season 7's densest hour: 76 jokes in 24 minutes of controlled absurdist chaos.
